newsitem.title: UK: S&P gives Moscow BB minus foreign currency rating.
newsitem.headline: S&P gives Moscow BB minus foreign currency rating.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Monday it had assigned a BB minus long-term foreign currency issuer credit rating to the City of Moscow.
The rating is constrained by the BB minus rating assigned to the Russian Federation's foreign curency debt, the agency said in a statement.
This is Standard & Poor's first local government rating in the Russian Federation.
S&P said the outlook was stable.
Following is a full press release from S&P.

Standard & Poor's today has assigned its double-B'-minus long-term foreign currency issuer credit rating to the City of Moscow. The rating is constrained by the double-B'-minus rating assigned to the Russian Federation's foreign curency debt.
This is Standard & Poor's first local government rating in the Russian Federation. The outlook is stable.
Moscow's rating is based on:
-- the capital city's increasingly diversified economy underpinned by the its role as the center for trade, services, education, finance and government within the Federation;
-- projected GDP growth in 1997 after significant declines due to a drop off in industrial output for 1994 and 1995;
-- strong budgetary performance with surplus operating and balanced capital accounts since 1991 (average operating surplus since 1994 equaled 39% of operating revenues);
-- no payment delays in wages (dissimilar to most governments in Russia);
-- prudent management committed both to the reform process and to maintaining strong financial performance through balanced budgets and limits on debt and;
-- low existing and planned debt (including the upcoming US$400 million Eurobond, direct debt equals 11% of budgeted operating revenues and below 5% of GDP).
Constraining factors are:
-- severe transitional pressures including growth in unemployment, a sizable shadow economy and weak tax collections;
-- unpredictable intergovernmental relationships including delays in payments from the Federation;
-- low revenue flexibility due to: tax rates and allocations set by the Federation, current utilization of maximum local rates, and an inability to raise fees since per capita wealth is low;
-- large capital expenditure needs in housing, health care, and environment protection;
-- significant contingent liabilities and trade creditors which have yet to be adequately assessed by the city.
OUTLOOK: Stable.

Although the country's transition process will continue to be uneven, Moscow will benefit from its comparatively strong base of diversified businesses and skilled workforce which have already attracted significant investment. Management's commitment to balanced budgets will preserve the strong financial position as debt plans remain moderate, Standard & Poor's said.
